In the usual (“one–body”) impulse approximation for a lepton–nucleus reaction one makes three, mutually reinforcing, simplifications.

• The external probe is assumed to couple to a single nucleon only; all many–body exchange currents are neglected.  
  → Assumption 1.

• The struck nucleon is taken to move and to be detected as if it were in free space; any binding potential that held it in the nucleus is ignored during (and after) the interaction.  
  → Assumption 4.

• One furthermore neglects any further interaction of the ejected nucleon with the spectators; the rest of the nucleus is considered “transparent.”  
  → Assumption 2.

These three statements together are what is normally meant by the (plane–wave) impulse approximation.  
Whether the quarks inside the nucleon are relativistic (Assumption 3) is irrelevant; the impulse approximation is formulated at the hadronic level and does not require any specific description of the nucleon’s internal quark dynamics.

Hence the set {1, 2, 4} is both necessary and sufficient, whereas Assumption 3 is extraneous.

Answer: C
